4. 
Perspectives on Substantial Evidence—Dickinson v. Zurko. In 
Dickinson v. Zurko, 527 U.S. 150 (1999), the Supreme Court discussed, the 
difference between appellate court review of lower court fact findings and 
judicial review of agency factual determinations. The issue in Dickinson was 
whether the Federal Circuit had correctly applied the judicial “clearly 
erroneous” standard in reviewing certain determinations of the Patent and 
Trademark Office or whether the court should, instead, have applied the APA’s 
“substantial evidence” standard. The Federal Circuit justified using the 
former, ostensibly less deferential, standard on the ground that it had applied 
the “clearly erroneous” long before the APA’s passage. It cited 5 U.S.C. § 559, 
which specifies that the APA “does not limit or repeal additional requirements 
* * * recognized by law.”
Writing for the Court, Justice Breyer was unpersuaded. He found unclear 
the pre-APA practice on which the Federal Circuit relied, and he reasoned that 
Congress had intended the APA to establish a uniform standard for judicial 
review of agency adjudications. In doing so. Justice Breyer described the 
difference between the two standards of review as follows:
This Court has described the APA court/agency “substantial 
evidence” standard as requiring a court to ask whether a “reasonable 
mind might accept” a particular evidentiary record as “adequate to 
support a conclusion.” Consolidated Edison v. NLRB, 305 U.S. 197 at 
229 (1938). It has described the court/court “clearly erroneous” 
standard in terms of whether a reviewing judge has a “definite and 
firm conviction” that an error has been committed. United States v. 
United States Gypsum Co., 333 U.S. 364, 395 (1948). And it has 
suggested that the former is somewhat less strict than the latter. 
Universal Camera, 340 U.S., at 477, 488. * * *
The upshot in terms of judicial review is some practical 
difference in outcome depending on which standard is used. The 
court/agency standard * * * is somewhat less strict than the court/ 
court standard. But the difference is a subtle one—so finft that (apart 
from the present case) we have failed to uncover a single instance in 
which a reviewing court conceded that use of one standard rather 
than the other would in fact have produced a different outcome.
b. Review of Factual Findings When the Substantial Evidence 
Test Does Not Apply
Under the APA, and many agency-specific statutes, the “substantial 
evidence” test apphes only when an agency determination is made in an 
on-the-record, formal proceeding. For instance, the “substantial evidence” 
standard contained in Section 706(2)(E) expressly apphes only to cases 
“subject to sections 556 and 557 ... or otherwise reviewed on the record of 
an agency hearing provided by statute,” i.e., formal proceedings under the 
APA. Yet agencies make factual determinations in many other contexts as
